shutdown_001:n1.prompt:
You are helping me begin winding down my company. Please draft the board of directors' written consent and the stockholders' written consent authorizing dissolution of the corporation under Delaware law (or the state of incorporation I specify). If you don't already have it, ask me for: the company's legal name, state and date of incorporation, entity type (C-corp/LLC), the names/titles of current directors and officers, the approximate cap table or list of stockholders eligible to vote, and any specific effective date I want for dissolution.

Using that information, prepare: (1) a board resolution recommending dissolution, approving the plan of dissolution, authorizing officers to file the certificate of dissolution, wind down affairs, pay/settle liabilities, and distribute remaining assets to stockholders after satisfying obligations; (2) a stockholder written consent approving the board's dissolution recommendation, referencing the required vote threshold under the certificate of incorporation and bylaws; and (3) a short cover memo summarizing next steps (tax clearance, creditor notice, asset distribution) so I have context.

Use plain, standard corporate legal drafting language consistent with typical Delaware dissolution consents. Clearly mark placeholder fields (names, dates, share counts) that I need to fill in or confirm. Do not send, file, or notarize anything, and do not sign on my behalf — these documents require actual director and stockholder signatures.

When done, give me: the three drafted documents in an easily reviewable format (e.g., text or markdown I can paste into a document), a short list of open items or missing information, and a note that these drafts remains a human step for legal review and signature. Then stop for human sign-off before any further action.

shutdown_001:n2.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the board and stockholder dissolution consents for shutting down my Delaware corporation. Before drafting, ask me for anything you need: my company's exact legal name, state of incorporation (Delaware), names and titles of all current directors, names of stockholders and their share counts/classes, the proposed effective date of dissolution, and any specific wind-up terms the board wants stated (e.g., appointment of a person to oversee wind-up, authorization to pay debts and distribute remaining assets, authorization to file the certificate of dissolution).

Using this information, draft two documents: (1) a Board of Directors' Written Consent approving dissolution of the corporation, authorizing the officers to file the Delaware certificate of dissolution, wind up affairs, pay liabilities, and distribute remaining assets, and recommending stockholder approval; (2) a Stockholders' Written Consent approving the dissolution as recommended by the board, referencing the required statutory vote threshold. Use standard corporate consent formatting with signature blocks for each director and stockholder, dated lines, and a recital of the relevant DGCL dissolution authority.

If I have an e-signature tool configured (e.g., DocuSign or similar), prepare the documents for upload and set up the signer routing (names/emails) so they are ready to send, but do not send them yet.

When the drafts and signer routing are ready, present them to me for review and stop for human sign-off — the directors and stockholders themselves must review and sign these consents, as this is a governance vote only they can give. Report back with the drafted documents, the proposed signer list, and a summary of any open items I need to confirm before signatures are collected.

shutdown_001:n3.prompt:
You are helping me run the final off-cycle payroll and terminate contractor engagements in {{vendor}} as part of shutting down the company. Ask me for anything you need: my {{vendor}} company/account identifier, the final work dates for employees and contractors, any final bonuses/severance amounts, and confirmation of which contractors are being paid out.

Using my configured credentials, do the following: (1) Retrieve upcoming/off-cycle payrolls for the company via the {{vendor}} API to locate or confirm the final payroll run. (2) For contractors, build and submit a contractor payment preview via the {{vendor}} API to validate final payment amounts before anything is finalized. (3) Compile a clear summary showing: final employee payroll totals (regular pay, severance/bonus, PTO payout if applicable), final contractor payment totals, the pay date, and any anomalies or discrepancies flagged in the preview (e.g., unexpected amounts, missing bank details, duplicate entries). (4) Note which contractors will be marked terminated/offboarded in {{vendor}} once the payment runs.

Do not submit or execute the final payroll run or contractor payments, and do not mark any contractor as terminated in the system yet. Present the full preview, totals, and anomaly list to me in your report, along with a checklist of the remaining actions (submit payroll, submit contractor payments, offboard contractors) so I can review dollar amounts and dates. Then stop for human sign-off before any payment is actually processed or any termination is finalized.

shutdown_001:n4.prompt:
You are helping me shut down the company by preparing the cancellation of all vendor contracts and subscriptions. Do not cancel or modify anything yet — this requires my explicit approval before any change is applied.

First, ask me for: (1) a list of all active vendors, SaaS subscriptions, and service providers (e.g., software tools, cloud hosting, insurance, office/co-working leases, payroll or HR platforms, marketing tools, professional services); (2) for each, the account owner/login contact, renewal or billing date, contract term/notice period, and any early-termination fees; (3) my company's legal name and effective wind-down date; (4) whether any vendors are already known to require special handling (e.g., data export before closure).

Using this information, build a single tracking sheet (table format) listing each vendor with: service name, monthly/annual cost, contract end date or required notice period, cancellation method (self-service portal, email, or phone), any data-export or final-invoice steps needed before cancellation, and target cancellation date. Flag any vendors with auto-renewal dates that are imminent so they can be prioritized.

Draft the specific cancellation notice or email for each vendor that requires written notice, pre-filled with company name, account details, and requested effective date, ready for me to send. Note any vendors where data must be exported or backed up first, and list that as a prerequisite step.

Compile the full checklist and all drafted notices, then stop for human sign-off — do not send cancellation requests, close accounts, or authorize any charges/refunds until I have reviewed and approved each item.

shutdown_001:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but not submit) the Delaware Certificate of Dissolution and franchise-tax true-up for our corporation as part of shutting down the company. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for any missing inputs: our exact corporate name as registered in Delaware, our Delaware file number, our EIN, the effective dissolution date approved by the board/stockholders, our registered agent's name and address, and our current Delaware franchise tax and annual report filing status (any amounts already paid or outstanding).
2. Go to https://corp.delaware.gov/corpforms/ and locate the Certificate of Dissolution form and any related franchise-tax payment/reporting requirements. Note the required fields, filing fee, and accepted payment methods.
3. Prepare a complete draft: fill in all form fields with the details I provided, and separately calculate/organize the franchise-tax true-up figures (final tax due through the dissolution date, using our Delaware franchise tax method — authorized shares or assumed par value — based on data I supply or that you find in our records).
4. Compile a short checklist covering: final franchise tax return filed and paid, all annual reports up to date, certificate of dissolution fields verified, registered agent confirmation, and payment method ready.
5. Present the completed draft certificate, the franchise-tax true-up calculation, and the checklist to me for review.

Do not submit the form, make any payment, or attest to any figures on my behalf — the franchise-tax attestation and authorization to dissolve are legally binding acts that only an officer can make, so you must stop for human sign-off once the draft and checklist are ready. Report back with the filled-in draft details, the tax calculation summary, the checklist, and a clear note that this remains a human step for final review, attestation, and submission.

shutdown_001:n6.prompt:
You are helping me monitor the status of our Delaware Certificate of Dissolution filing while we wind down the company. The actual acceptance and processing of the filing by the Delaware Secretary of State remains a human step — the state's internal review and turnaround time is outside our control and there is no interface for you to drive to speed it up or force completion.

Please do the following preparatory and monitoring work instead:

1. Ask me for: the date we submitted the Certificate of Dissolution, the confirmation or filing number (if any) we received from Delaware, the method of filing (mail, online portal, or via a registered agent/filing service), and whether we used a registered agent service to submit it.
2. If a Delaware Division of Corporations entity search or status-check page is accessible, check the current status of our entity using the entity name or file number I provide, and record what it shows (e.g., 'active,' 'dissolution pending,' 'dissolved').
3. Draft a short status-check email or message I can send to our registered agent or the Delaware Division of Corporations asking them to confirm receipt and expected processing time for our dissolution filing.
4. Set up a simple tracking note (date checked, status observed, next check date) so we have a record of when we verified status, and suggest a reasonable interval for re-checking (e.g., every 5–7 business days) given typical state processing times.
5. Flag to me clearly that once the certificate is accepted, the next steps (franchise tax true-up confirmation, state withdrawals, etc.) can proceed, but that confirmation of acceptance itself is a third-party wait and cannot be completed or accelerated by you.

Report back with: the entity status you found (if checkable), the drafted status-check message, the tracking note format, and a recommended next check-in date. Do not attempt to submit any filings, sign documents, or represent to the state that dissolution is complete.

shutdown_001:n7.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for our CPA to complete the company's final federal and state tax returns as part of dissolving the corporation. Please assist by gathering and organizing everything the CPA will need, but do not calculate final tax figures, gain/loss on distributions, or make any tax judgment calls yourself — that requires a licensed CPA's professional determination.

First, ask me for anything missing: our company legal name, EIN, state(s) of incorporation and registration, the planned/actual dissolution date, our accounting software or bookkeeping system access, the CPA firm's name and contact, and where our financial records are stored.

Then: (1) compile a checklist of documents the CPA will need — year-to-date profit & loss, balance sheet as of dissolution date, general ledger, fixed asset schedule, prior-year returns, records of any asset distributions to shareholders, final payroll reports, and outstanding liabilities; (2) pull and organize these records from our accounting system into a single shared folder or export, labeling each file clearly; (3) draft an email to the CPA summarizing the dissolution date, requesting preparation of the final federal Form 1120 (or applicable entity return) marked as 'final return,' final state return(s), and IRS account closure, and asking what additional information they need; (4) note in the email that shareholder distribution details and final gain/loss figures are pending their professional calculation.

Done looks like: a complete, organized document package, a drafted (unsent) email to the CPA ready for my review, and a checklist of open items awaiting their figures. Since finalizing the tax calculations requires licensed judgment, stop for human sign-off before sending anything to the CPA or filing. Report back with the checklist, the folder/export location, and the drafted email text for my review.

shutdown_001:n8.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but NOT sign or file) the final IRS documents needed to close out our corporation: the final federal and state tax return jurats, and IRS Form 966 (Corporate Dissolution or Liquidation). This is part of shutting down the company.

Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: our EIN, the corporation's exact legal name and address, the state of incorporation (Delaware), the date the board/stockholders adopted the dissolution resolution, the planned or actual date of dissolution/liquidation, the accountant or tax preparer's contact info, and copies or drafts of the final federal and state tax returns.

Your job:
1. Confirm with me (or our accountant) that the final tax returns are complete and marked 'final return.'
2. Pre-fill a draft of Form 966 with all required fields: corporate name, EIN, address, date of incorporation, date resolution was adopted, date of dissolution, and a summary of the resolution/plan of dissolution language, leaving the officer signature line blank.
3. Prepare a checklist confirming: which officer is authorized to sign, where the jurat pages are located in the final returns, and any deadlines (Form 966 is due within 30 days of the resolution's adoption).
4. Assemble all documents into a single packet (digital or printable) ready for the officer's review and signature.

Do not attest, sign, e-file, or submit any of these documents — only an authorized officer can make the perjury-backed attestation. Once the packet and checklist are ready, stop for human sign-off.

Report back with: a summary of what was prepared, the location/filenames of the drafts, the checklist of open items, and confirmation that everything is staged and awaiting the officer's signature.

shutdown_001:n9.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the final IRS filings and account closure request as part of shutting down my company. Please work from the IRS guidance page 'Closing a Business' (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/closing-a-business). If you don't already have them, ask me for: our EIN, entity type, final tax year-end date, the state of incorporation (Delaware), the date the business ceased operations/dissolved, whether we had employees (for final Forms 940/941), whether we issued 1099s to contractors this year, and our registered mailing address.

Actions to take:
1. Identify and list every final return required for our entity type (e.g., final federal income tax return checked as 'final', final employment tax returns if we had employees, final Form 1099 filings for contractors, and any other IRS forms flagged as needed when closing a business).
2. Draft a written IRS account closure request letter that includes our EIN, entity legal name, business address, and reason for closing, formatted for either mailing or transmission by a credentialed e-file preparer.
3. Prepare a checklist confirming which final returns have been drafted, which need my review of figures, and what supporting documents (final balance sheet, payroll totals, 1099 totals) are still needed.
4. Note that actual transmission of e-filed returns requires a credentialed e-file practitioner system, and the closure letter must be physically signed and mailed — both of these remain a human step that you cannot complete.
5. Include instructions for how I (or my accountant) can later verify IRS processing/account closure status.

When done, report back: the list of required final forms, the drafted closure letter text, the outstanding data/documents needed from me, and the remains a human step transmission/mailing task. Then stop for human sign-off before anything is submitted or mailed.

shutdown_001:n10.prompt:
You are helping me withdraw our corporation's foreign-state registrations as part of dissolving the company. We are a Delaware corporation registered to do business as a foreign entity in one or more other states.

First, ask me for: (1) the full legal company name, (2) Delaware entity/file number, (3) the complete list of states where we are registered as a foreign entity, and (4) confirmation that our Delaware certificate of dissolution (or good-standing status) is in hand, since most states require a certificate of good standing or proof of dissolution from Delaware attached to the withdrawal filing.

For each state on the list, do the following: locate that state's Secretary of State (or equivalent business filing agency) online portal; find the 'withdrawal of foreign registration' (sometimes called 'certificate of withdrawal' or 'application for withdrawal of authority') form; log in using our configured credentials where an account is required; fill in all required fields (entity name, Delaware file number, effective date of withdrawal, registered agent info, and any tax-clearance attestation the state requires); attach the Delaware certificate of dissolution/good standing if the portal accepts uploads; and calculate the filing fee for each state.

Do not submit any filing or pay any fee — prepare each state's withdrawal form fully filled out and ready to file, and stop for human sign-off before submission.

Report back a table listing each state, the portal URL, the filing fee, any prerequisite documents still needed (e.g., state tax clearance certificates), and the status of each prepared form (ready to submit vs. blocked, with reason).

shutdown_001:n11.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the final bank account closure and asset distribution for our company as part of dissolving the corporation. Our banking vendor is {{vendor}}. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) the {{vendor}} account details, (2) the final list of creditors/vendors still owed money and amounts, (3) the shareholder distribution list with amounts per the dissolution plan, and (4) any outstanding checks, invoices, or payroll/contractor obligations that must clear first.

Using {{vendor}}'s portal, please:
1. Use universal search to pull a complete transaction history and confirm no pending/unresolved charges, subscriptions, or holds remain on the accounts.
2. Generate and save a bank verification letter and record the account/routing numbers for our records before closure.
3. Draft a prioritized payout worksheet: first creditor/vendor payments via ACH or wire, then any remaining contractor/payroll obligations, then shareholder distributions — each with recipient, amount, method, and account/routing info pre-filled and ready to submit.
4. Check and note the status of any pending account applications or transfers still under review.
5. Prepare (but do not submit) the ACH/wire payment batches for creditor payments and shareholder distributions, and draft the account closure request.

Do not initiate any transfers, submit payment batches, or close the accounts yourself. Distribution amounts and creditor priority require an authorized officer's judgment under state dissolution and fiduciary rules, so this remains a human step — you must stop for human sign-off once the worksheet, verification letter, and draft payment batches are ready.

Report back with: the verification letter, the finalized payout worksheet showing creditor and shareholder amounts, confirmation of no pending obligations, and the draft closure request, clearly flagged as pending my approval.

shutdown_001:n12.prompt:
You are helping me archive our corporate records for long-term retention as part of dissolving the company. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) which {{vendor}} cloud-storage account to use (confirm you have configured credentials for it), (2) the list of source locations/folders containing corporate records (e.g., board minutes, stockholder consents, cap table, contracts, payroll/tax filings, dissolution filings, bank statements), and (3) the retention duration or policy we need to satisfy (many states/advisors recommend 7+ years).

Actions to take:
1. Use {{vendor}}'s list/search API to compile a full inventory of the corporate records to be archived from the specified source locations.
2. Create a clearly named top-level archive folder (e.g., '[CompanyName]-Corporate-Records-Archive-[Year]').
3. Upload each record into that folder via {{vendor}}'s file upload/create API, using resumable/chunked upload for large files where supported.
4. Where {{vendor}} supports it, attach metadata or tags indicating document category and retention classification, and confirm version history/revision retention is enabled for these files.
5. Set restrictive access permissions or collaboration settings on the archive folder so only authorized parties (e.g., former officers, counsel) can access it, consistent with our retention policy.
6. Verify completeness by re-listing/searching the archive folder and cross-checking against your original inventory; flag any missing or failed uploads.
7. Confirm export capability — note that all archived files can later be exported in open formats if we need to leave {{vendor}}.

Done looks like: every identified corporate record is uploaded into the named archive folder, tagged/classified where possible, access is restricted appropriately, and a verification pass confirms the archive matches the inventory with no gaps.

Report back: the archive folder location/link, total record count archived vs. inventoried, any files that failed to upload or are missing, the permission/access settings applied, and confirmation that retention/versioning is enabled.
